headline: Mathan Somasundaram holds REA Group as a quality business but warns against fresh buying amid cycle uncertainty and growth-to-value rotation pressure.

He sees uncertainty in the property market, with turnover slowing — analogising it to the pre-GFC lull in 2006. He expects the stock to struggle in the short to medium term but sees opportunity once there is clarity on the economy. His recommendation: if you already hold it, stay; if deploying fresh money, wait.
quote: Look, I think it's a phenomenally good business. It's one of the, um, the old text. Um, look, it's probably the better of the three as well. Um, so, look, it's it's a great business. It's just in the wrong side of the cycle. Um, there's going to be uncertainty. The market's going to wait and see how this plays out. In Australia, we've had nearly two years of growth to value rotation. And I think that will continue with bond yields where they are. So growth stocks are going to be under pressure. So I think Aria will remain under pressure... I think short to medium term is still going to be a bit volatile, and then the market is going to be uncertain. So I suspect the stock's going to struggle in the short to medium term. But once we have some stability and we have some I suppose clarity on where the economy is headed in the medium to long term. Then I think things will start to run back and there'll be an opportunity. So okay, I like it, but I'm not buying it right now. So if you're there, you can hold it. If you've been there for a run, then you don't care. It's a good quality business. You can hold it, but fresh money. I'll probably wait.

headline: Nathan Somerson-Darren advises against fresh money in Tasmania at $2.4 billion market cap, flagging that growth-by-acquisition becomes exponentially harder at scale.

For holders who have done very well, taking capital off the table and running the rest is the prudent approach; no fresh money.
quote: The multiples are massive. It's barely getting any yield. So you're buying the growth and it is growth by acquisition. So you're betting on management doing good acquisition... when you're a two point four billion market cap, your ability to deliver that kind of performance that you've seen in the last couple of years, again, is very hard... once you get to that two point three billion, you have to do big acquisition to make them valid to drive the growth. Now, when you're doing big and big acquisitions, then you get into that risky play... if you're there, well done. You picked a great winner. Write it. headline: Nathan Somerson-Darren is structurally bullish gold driven by central bank demand, US fiscal deterioration, global deleveraging risks, and expected AUD weakness.
reasoning: Central banks globally, led by China, are buying gold as an alternative reserve asset to the USD, driven by concern about the US dollar's long-term viability given unsustainable debt dynamics. The US debt is being driven by deficits which are themselves driven by interest payments on the debt — a self-reinforcing negative cycle. Central banks have no choice but to expand balance sheets and try to suppress bond yields, a dynamic that is inherently gold-positive. The Australian dollar is likely to weaken with global growth, adding a currency tailwind for Australian gold producers. A global deleveraging cycle is underway, with China having already burst its property bubble and Australia moving to curb its own property cycle.
quote: I don't see US having any real plans of sorting out their debt. Their debt is literally being driven by their deficit, which is literally being driven by the interest payment on the debt. So it's a self-sustaining growth model of the wrong kind... the central banks have no other option but to expand balance sheet and try and curb the bond yields because the bond market does not buy the spin from the government. Bond yields are rising around the world and everyone is trying to buy their bonds to curb the bond yields. So it's a cycle that is creating a problem. There's a reason why China basically blew up their property market because there was a global deleveraging cycle coming. And now the Australian government has moved to curb the property cycle because of the potential risk of what the deleveraging cycle can play out. So that's coming and the central banks will have to expand balance sheet to defend it. So in that context, gold is going to continue to outperform.
